p1.title: Passage 1
paras: The co-existence of high youth unemployment alongside widespread corporate talent shortages reveals a deep structural mismatch between formal educational curricula and the fast-evolving needs of the modern labor market. Academic institutions remain stubbornly tethered to legacy rote-learning systems that prioritize theoretical memorization over practical, dynamic problem-solving and technical fluency. As industrial sectors rapidly transform through automation, data analytics, and green engineering, graduates enter the workforce with obsolete skill sets, rendering them functionally unemployable despite holding formal degrees. Resolving this structural employment bottleneck requires a fundamental overhaul of vocational training, moving away from low-tier manual training toward high-value technical and cognitive skill development. This transformation requires deep institutional partnerships between universities and industries, ensuring that apprenticeships, real-world project learning, and adaptive digital skills are deeply integrated into curricula. Youth employment strategies must look beyond simply increasing graduation rates, focusing instead on building a highly agile, continuously upskilling workforce capable of navigating continuous industrial disruption.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: For generations the mangrove forests that fringe tropical coasts were regarded as wasteland: muddy, mosquito-ridden and of no obvious use except as a source of firewood. Their clearance for ports, prawn farms and seaside construction was seen as improvement. Only in recent decades has a fuller accounting begun to emerge. The tangled roots of mangroves trap sediment and slow the force of waves, so that villages behind a healthy belt of mangroves suffer markedly less damage from cyclones and storm surges than those whose shoreline has been cleared. The same roots shelter the young of many fish and crabs, sustaining fisheries far beyond the forest's edge. Mangrove soils, moreover, lock away carbon at rates that exceed those of many inland forests.

Restoration has become fashionable, and planting campaigns now produce impressive photographs of volunteers pressing seedlings into the mud. Results have been mixed. Seedlings planted on mudflats where mangroves never naturally grew, or of a single species chosen for convenience, frequently die within a year. Successful projects tend to be less photogenic: they restore the tidal flow that was blocked by embankments, allow nature to reseed the area, and involve the fishing communities who have the strongest reason to protect the forest once it returns.

questions.q: The simultaneous existence of youth unemployment and corporate talent shortages is, according to the author, proof of:
opts: A structural mismatch between curricula and market needs.
The failure of job portals to track vacancies.
A drop in the number of students taking degrees.
Companies refusing to pay fair wages.
questions.why: Detail: the first sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Traditional academic institutions are criticized for prioritizing:
opts: Green engineering over business management.
Rote learning and theoretical memorization over practical problem-solving.
Continuous upskilling with industry.
Technical fluency and project-based learning.
questions.why: Detail: the second sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: According to the passage, why are many degree holders "functionally unemployable"?
opts: They lack capital to start businesses.
Universities have replaced theory with apprenticeships.
Automation has removed all human jobs.
They graduate with obsolete skills that do not match industry needs.
questions.why: Detail: the third sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: To resolve the employment bottleneck, vocational training must:
opts: Shift toward high-value technical and cognitive skills.
Focus only on low-tier manual skills.
Be cut off from industry input.
Spend more time on rote learning.
questions.why: Detail: the fourth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The ultimate goal of youth employment strategies should be to:
opts: Maximise graduation numbers without changing curricula.
Stop industries from automating.
Build an agile, continuously upskilling workforce.
Subsidise firms that hire untrained graduates.
questions.why: Main idea: the last sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: How to Photograph Coastal Forests
Why Inland Forests Store More Carbon
Mangroves: From Wasteland to Coastal Guardian
The Profits of Prawn Farming
questions.why: Main idea: mangroves 'were regarded as wasteland', but a 'fuller accounting' shows they protect coasts, fisheries and carbon.

questions.q: Which benefit of mangroves is mentioned in the passage?
opts: They provide fertile soil for growing rice.
They raise water temperature to help prawn farms.
They eliminate mosquitoes from coastal areas.
They reduce the damage that storm surges cause to villages behind them.
questions.why: Detail: villages behind mangroves 'suffer markedly less damage from cyclones and storm surges'.

questions.q: The reference to 'impressive photographs of volunteers' suggests that the author believes:
opts: planting campaigns always succeed within a year.
some restoration efforts value appearance over ecological success.
volunteers should not take part in restoration.
photographs are the best measure of a project's success.
questions.why: Inference: 'Results have been mixed', and 'successful projects tend to be less photogenic', implying visible campaigns are not necessarily effective.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards mangrove restoration is best described as:
opts: indifferent to whether restoration succeeds.
uncritically enthusiastic about all planting drives.
wholly opposed to restoration efforts.
supportive of restoration but critical of poorly designed campaigns.
questions.why: Tone: the author praises projects that restore tidal flow and involve fishing communities, while noting that convenient single-species planting 'frequently die within a year'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'photogenic' means:
opts: attractive or striking when photographed
costly to carry out
sensitive to light
proven by scientific study
questions.why: Vocabulary: successful projects are 'less photogenic' than campaigns that 'produce impressive photographs'.
